text: Residents cheer as the new city park opens. Mayor cuts the ribbon with a giant pair of scissors and a suspiciously large smile.
Families flock to the freshly planted park. Local ducks report they have never been so well fed.
A new park breaks ground downtown. Our reporter asks a pigeon for comment; it simply says, "Finally, a bench."
The park is open! Joggers are thrilled, couch potatoes are furious, and the lawn is already being rolled out.
Mayor unveils the city's newest green space. Critics admit the swings are strangely comfortable.
Sunshine, grass, and a brand-new fountain. The new park has officially made our city 12 percent more relaxing.
The new school opens its doors today. Students arrive with backpacks, nervous smiles, and the faint smell of fresh paint.
Parents celebrate a brand-new school in the neighbourhood. The school bus driver promises to learn everyone's name by Friday.
Education gets a boost as the city's newest school welcomes its first class. The chalkboards are reportedly still shiny.
A new school is complete, and the principal says the library smells like a brand-new book. We agree, it is lovely.
Local kids react to the new school with enthusiasm. One eight-year-old asks if homework is included in the price.
The new hospital opens its emergency wing this morning. Doctors say they are ready for anything, including the cafeteria pudding.
A brand-new hospital is open for business. Ambulance drivers report the shortest trips they have had all year.
Health officials celebrate the city's new hospital. Waiting rooms are full, but at least the chairs are comfortable.
The hospital ribbon is cut and the first patients are admitted. Nurses ask the public to please stop waving at the MRI machine.
Residents sleep easier knowing a full hospital now stands in the city. Local hypochondriacs are already booking appointments.
The new library opens its shelves to the public. The librarian asks everyone to whisper, politely, and only about the books.
A quiet triumph: the city library is finally open. Bookworms report a sudden desire to stay indoors on purpose.
Reading levels are expected to rise after the grand opening of the city library. The overdue fines will rise too, we are told.
The stadium is complete and the crowd is roaring. The mayor throws the first ball, misses the goal, and still gets a standing ovation.
Fans pour into the brand-new stadium for opening night. Hot dog sales have already broken a city record.
The city has a stadium! Local sports fans weep openly, then immediately buy season tickets.
The city treasury is in the black this quarter. The finance office has been asked to stop smiling in public meetings.
Good news for the wallet: a budget surplus has been announced. Councillors are already arguing about which fountain to fund.
Tax coffers are overflowing. Economists call it a miracle; the mayor calls it excellent planning.
The city ends the year with money left over. Residents are asked to stop being shocked about it.
Crime rates fall for the third month in a row. Police credit better lighting, better patrols, and one very well-behaved goose.
Streets feel safer as crime drops across the city. Shop owners say they can finally leave the door unlocked, sort of.
Police report a quiet week, the quietest in a decade. Officers admit they are a little bored and enjoying it.
The city has reached 1,000 residents! A small crowd gathers to greet the one-thousandth citizen, who is mildly confused.
Milestone reached: our town officially has a thousand people. The mayor promises a sign, a parade, and a second sign.
Ten thousand residents! The city is now big enough to have traffic jams, and the citizens are proud of it.
The census clerk has been busy. Ten thousand people now call this city home, and most of them are asking for parking.
Fifty thousand residents! Our city is growing up fast, and the newspaper finally needs a second page for the obituaries.
Unemployment falls to a record low. Job seekers are rare, employers are nervous, and the coffee shops are very busy.
Jobs are plentiful this season. Local employers report they are competing for workers with the cats in the warehouse.
A new survey finds residents are happier than ever. Asked why, most people said the bins were collected on time.
Happiness levels climb across the city. One resident says, "I don't know why, but I keep smiling at strangers."
The new transit line opens today. Commuters squeeze onto the first trip, grinning like children on a field trip.
Public transport gets a boost as the new route goes live. Buses are on time, and drivers are shocked about it too.
The bus depot opens its gates. The first bus rolls out in a cloud of diesel and quiet pride.
A new bus depot is operational. Mechanics say the buses are already more polished than most of the city's cars.
The rail depot is open for business. Engineers wave from the platform, and the first train whistles with obvious pride.
Trains finally have a home. The new rail depot opens to cheers, and a sprinkling of tears from the signal operator.
The tram depot is complete. Trams glide out for their first run, bells clanging like an eager school choir.
A new taxi depot opens in town. Drivers report that the radio is working, and the meter is finally honest.
A new bus stop opens on Main Street. The bench is comfortable, the shelter is dry, and the timetable is almost accurate.
The power grid has spare capacity to spare. Electricians are seen smiling with their hands in their pockets.
The reservoir is full and the taps are running freely. Plumbers everywhere report a quieter week.
Every residential plot is now occupied. New homes are flying up, and the furniture shops are sending thank-you cards.
The shopping district is fully built. Shopkeepers report the first queue of customers they have seen in years.
Factories are humming on every industrial plot. The smoke is a bit thick, but the paychecks are thicker.
Traffic is flowing smoothly through the city centre. Drivers are suspicious, but they are not complaining.
Housing is affordable and plentiful this quarter. Landlords are asked, politely, to keep their hands in their pockets.
A new poll puts the mayor well ahead. The mayor thanks voters, then quietly asks the pollster for a second opinion.
The city has fully recovered from last month's disaster. Volunteers are honoured with a parade and an extremely long lunch.
Crews finish the big city clean-up. Streets sparkle, the gutters gleam, and the seagulls are deeply offended.
Hundreds of new trees are planted along the avenues. Local birds have already filed a complaint about the lack of nesting space, but they are thrilled.
The river is clean enough for fish to return. A fisherman catches a trout and asks the reporter, "What took you so long?"
Graduation rates climb to a new high. Teachers say their students are the most curious and the most annoying in the state, in the best way.
Smog hangs over the industrial district. Residents are advised to stay indoors, which is hard when the pizza delivery is outside.
Air quality hits a dangerous low. Health officials urge people to wear masks, and the mask shops are sold out in an hour.
The city's skyline is barely visible through the haze. Tourists take photos of the fog and ask if it is always like this.
Pollution levels spike again. The mayor blames the weather, the weather blames the factories, and the factories blame the trucks.
A traffic jam stretches for nine kilometres. Drivers have started a neighbourly barbecue on the motorway.
Gridlock grips the city centre. Commuters are now reading novels in their cars and some have finished them.
The morning commute becomes an endurance test. One driver has been stuck at the same junction since breakfast and is now a local legend.
The city is running a deficit. Councillors have been asked to stop buying new fountains and start counting coins.
Treasury reports red ink across every department. The finance director has asked for a holiday, and has been refused.
Money is tight at City Hall. The mayor insists everything is fine, while the photocopier quietly stops working.
Crime jumps this week, with several break-ins reported on the east side. Residents are asked to lock doors and not leave bikes outside.
Police are stretched thin after a spike in thefts. A local shopkeeper says he has now chased three hats and a shopping trolley.
A fire breaks out in the old warehouse district. Firefighters are working through the night, and the toast in the nearby café is burnt.
Smoke fills the streets as a blaze tears through a block of flats. Everyone is safe, but the flats are not.
A power cut plunges half the city into darkness. People gather on their doorsteps to talk to each other, and some are enjoying it.
The lights go out across the north side. Engineers say the fault is being fixed, and the ice cream in the freezers is not.
Water pressure drops across the city. Residents are asked to stop washing cars, and several cars look suspiciously clean anyway.
A water shortage hits the eastern neighbourhoods. Shower schedules are now being negotiated over the fence.
Unemployment rises sharply this month. Job centres are busy, and the job-seekers' queue is out the door and round the block.
Jobs are scarce and tempers are short. Local cafes report the same customers all day, all of them updating their CVs.
Workers walk out across the city. Picket lines are polite, the tea is hot, and nobody is sure when it will end.
A transport strike grounds the buses. Commuters have dusted off their bicycles and are not happy about the hills.
The landfill is full. The city is now looking for somewhere else to put last year's sofas, which are still there.
Waste collectors are out of space. The rubbish is piling up on the high street and the seagulls have declared it a holiday.
Flood waters rise across the low districts. Residents move their cars to the hills and their cats to the attic.
Heavy rain swells the river and floods several streets. Boats are the only way to reach the bakery, which is now also a fish shop.
A survey shows residents are unhappier than last year. Asked for a reason, many simply said, "Have you seen the roads?"
Morale is low across the city. The mayor's approval rating is in free fall, and so is the pastry shop's rating.
Rents jump again this month. Tenants are sharing bedrooms and landlords are buying second yachts.
Housing costs soar across the city. One renter has moved into a shed and insists it has a view of the cathedral.
Factory chimneys belch black smoke over the east side. Residents are asking whether the paychecks are worth the cough.
Residents complain about constant noise from the industrial park. The factory foreman replies that noise is what progress sounds like.
Sleep is becoming a luxury in the city. Several neighbours have started leaving passive-aggressive notes on the factory gate.
A sewage leak forces the closure of a popular riverside walk. The ducks have filed a formal protest.
A road collapses on the main avenue, swallowing a parked van. The van driver is fine, but he is taking the bus to work today.
A bus route sits almost empty each morning. Drivers report that the only passenger is a pensioner who sings the whole way.
Homelessness rises in the city centre. Charities are asking for help, and the council is asking charities for patience.
A procurement scandal rocks City Hall. The contract for the new fountain was awarded to the mayor's cousin's pet shop.
Questions are raised over several suspicious contracts. The mayor insists the paperwork was simply very confusing.
The transit authority is running out of money. Bus tickets are now being paid for in biscuits, and the biscuits are running low.
Illegal dumping is found behind the old factory. A local man has been arrested after the investigation found a bathtub, a piano, and a goat.
A tram derails near the market square. Passengers are shaken but unhurt, and the tram is now a popular photo spot.
Smoke pours from the depot after a fire in the maintenance shed. Two buses are damaged, and the bus driver's lunch is gone.
A line of breakdowns stalls the city's fleet this morning. The mechanics are working flat out and their tea is going cold.
Homes are now sitting right beside the factory. Residents are reporting that the windows rattle and the curtains smell of soot.
A new factory opens beside a quiet neighbourhood. Neighbours say the view has changed from trees to chimneys overnight.
Planners place a factory right next to the terraces. Residents are demanding a hedge, a fence, and an apology.
Families are thrilled that the new park sits right next to their homes. The commute to the swings is now measured in seconds.
Houses along the park are selling fast. Estate agents are calling the view the greenest in the city.
Shoppers are taking their lunch breaks on the new park benches beside the shops. The sandwich sellers are doing a roaring trade.
A factory is built next to the primary school. Teachers have started closing the windows and teaching the children to hold their breath.
A new park borders the school playground. Teachers say lessons are shorter because the children keep running off to play.
A factory is placed beside the hospital. Doctors are asking planners whether the wards can have air filters, a fence, or both.
Patients now have a garden view from the new hospital ward. Doctors say recovery times are dropping, and so is the moaning.
The bus depot is now beside the houses. Residents report that the morning engine warm-ups start at dawn and never stop.
A bus depot opens next to the shopping street. Shopkeepers are delighted by the new crowds, though the diesel smell is a bit of a surprise.
The new rail depot sits right behind the terraced houses. Residents say the late-night shunting is practising for a very loud symphony.
A rail depot is wedged between the park and the playground. The swings now come with a soundtrack of screeching brakes.
The rail depot sits next to the shopping district and commuters are flooding in. The shops are doing so well they are asking for a bigger sign.
A power plant goes up next to the family homes. Residents are glad of the cheap electricity but mourn the view of the sky.
A new water tower stands beside the estate, and taps are running stronger than ever. The tower is also ideal for an ambitious graffiti artist.
Shops open right beside the new stadium. Match-day crowds have turned the high street into a carnival.
The stadium stands next to the houses. Residents can now hear every goal, including the ones from the pub on the corner.
The airport expansion now reaches the back gardens. Residents are teaching their dogs to stop barking at the planes.
Travellers flock to the new hotels beside the airport. Business is booming, and so is the coffee queue.
The landfill now sits next to the estate. The seagulls are settling in, and the smell has become a neighbourhood topic.
A fire station opens beside the residential streets. Families sleep a little easier knowing the engines are nearby.
A police station opens beside the high street. Shopkeepers say the shoplifters have all gone quiet and polite.
The tram depot is tucked neatly beside the park. Children wave at the trams and the drivers wave back.
The school and the shopping centre are now neighbours. Ice cream sales have tripled and the dentists are nervous.
The new park sits right beside the factory. Visitors are impressed by the flowers, then slightly sad about the smoke.
Shops now sit beside the factory. Shoppers complain about the soot on their shopping bags, but they keep coming back.
Shops and homes are now neighbours. Residents can buy bread without leaving the street, and the bakery is very pleased.
The hospital and school now stand side by side. Nurses and teachers are sharing a very long lunch break.
The hospital has been built next to the landfill. Staff are asking for better bins, better air, and a new hospital.
A power plant now looms over the school yard. Pupils have started calling the chimney Big Steve and drawing it in every lesson.
A quiet park is placed by the new houses. The estate agent calls it a lifestyle feature, and the residents call it heaven.
Local man wins a pie-eating contest and immediately asks for a second, larger trophy.
A goat is found wandering the high street wearing a tiny scarf. Its owner has not yet been identified.
Weather forecasters admit they were wrong again. The sun is shining, and so is every umbrella shop.
Local cafe launches a new coffee flavour called Monday. Customers describe it as bitter and inevitable.
A flock of pigeons is seen forming a neat queue at the bus stop. Transport officials are looking into it.
The city's oldest tree has been given a name. Residents are calling it Gerald, and Gerald is not impressed.
A street musician plays the same three notes all day. Locals say they have never felt so calm, or so trapped.
Council announces a new public holiday to celebrate the cheese festival. The cheese has not yet been consulted.
A bakery sells out of bread in under an hour. The baker says he has never been so popular, or so tired.
Residents report a strange smell near the harbour. Scientists say it is probably just the sea, doing its best.
A cat is spotted sitting on the mayor's chair during a council meeting. The cat has not been asked to leave.
Local school hosts a spelling bee. The winning word was 'mayor', which has raised a few eyebrows.
A man has spent three weeks painting a single bench. It is now the most beautiful bench in the city, and nobody can sit on it.
A kite gets stuck on the cathedral spire. Firefighters say they will rescue it as soon as it stops waving.
The city's oldest bus driver celebrates forty years on the job. He says the passengers have changed, but the potholes have not.
A snail has been seen crossing Main Street at a pace that has stopped traffic for twenty minutes. Drivers are patient, mostly.
Local choir announces a concert about bins. Tickets are free, which is a relief for everyone who has ever paid council tax.
A lost wallet is returned to its owner with a note that says, 'Next time, try a bigger pocket.'
A mysterious hole appears in the middle of the square. By lunchtime it has been filled with rubbish and a small tree.
Cyclists demand a bike lane on every street. The council demands a cycle helmet on every councillor.
A local dog is awarded a medal for guarding a sandwich for six hours. The sandwich has been recovered and is only slightly damp.
A tourist asks a shopkeeper where the famous landmark is. The shopkeeper points at the tourist and says, 'You're standing on it.'
A window cleaner reports a record number of pigeon complaints. The pigeons have declined to comment.
The city's amateur astronomers spot a bright light in the sky. It turns out to be the new billboard on Hill Road.
Local bakers challenge the city to a bread-off. Judges are still deciding what counts as a crust.
A small boy sells lemonade outside the town hall and accidentally raises more money than the entire parks budget.
A postman claims he has delivered letters to every house in town, twice. The letters are mostly complaints about the postman.
Citizens debate whether the city fountain should be a fountain or a statue. The fountain has not yet expressed a view.
A grandmother wins a national crossword competition using only the word 'bins'. Officials say the answer was technically correct.
The local radio station has announced a new weather forecast: mostly weather, with a chance of more weather.
A barber opens a shop at the top of the hill and promises a haircut with a view. Early customers report the view is excellent.
A school class plants a sunflower that grows taller than the town hall. The mayor asks it to keep its head down.
A newly built bridge is closed for an afternoon after a duck refuses to leave the middle of the road.
A council meeting ends early after a councillor falls asleep and starts a very convincing snore recording.
Local hardware shop sells out of umbrellas, then all of its sunglasses, and then starts selling umbrellas again.
A chess club reports a surge in membership after a grandmaster visits the library and wins every game in one afternoon.
Residents spot a hot-air balloon drifting above the rooftops. The pilot calls it a shortcut and asks for directions.
The bus timetable is now a work of fiction, according to passengers who have waited for it since Tuesday.
A town clock stops at quarter past four and nobody has been brave enough to fix it. The pub has kept the same time all week.
Local bowling club challenges the city to a match. The city has asked for a referee, a lawyer, and a rematch.
Teenagers launch a petition for a skate park. It is signed by everyone in town, including the skateboard.
A pensioner is seen cycling backwards down the high street to raise money for the library. The library is delighted.
Mysterious lights are seen over the reservoir. The water board confirms they are the new floating solar panels, and nobody is convinced.
A local delivery van is found parked in the middle of the square with a note reading 'Be back in five minutes.' It is still there.
Doctors announce a new spring cold is spreading across the city. Its main symptom is sneezing at council meetings.
A squirrel is elected onto the neighbourhood committee after receiving 400 nut-based votes.
A violinist plays in the middle of a traffic jam and the jam dissolves into applause within ten minutes.
A town-wide game of hide and seek ends when the mayor is found hiding in the recycling bin.
Local bakery introduces a loaf named after the mayor. Sales are strong, and the crust is very hard to bite.
A visiting magician makes the entire council disappear for twenty minutes. Residents report it was the most productive session in years.
A cloud shaped like a giant teapot hangs over the park all afternoon. Forecasters say it is not their fault.
The council unveils a new logo, which looks suspiciously like the logo of a bakery two streets away.
A market trader sells a bag of marbles for the price of a bag of gold. He says the gold will be very useful for the marbles.
Residents gather for the annual fun run. The winner completes the course, turns around, and runs it again out of enthusiasm.
A hedge is trimmed into the shape of a bus. Transport officials are not sure whether it counts as a new route.
A baker's apprentice accidentally makes 500 identical pies. The town has agreed to eat them, and is currently regretting it.
A charity sale of old furniture reveals a sofa that has been missing since 1997. It is still lumpy.
A window on the top floor of the town hall has been open all week. The council says it is a deliberate ventilation policy.
Local pub hosts a quiz night. The winning team is named 'Pub Quiz Night' and has never lost, because nobody else showed up.
Scientists confirm the city's pigeons have been practising for a flying display. It starts at noon tomorrow, nobody is sure why.
A children's puppet show is cancelled after the puppet of the mayor refuses to stop talking about the budget.
A stray balloon floats over the city and is adopted by an elderly couple. The balloon has since been named Doris.
The post office introduces a new stamp featuring a smiling rubber duck. Collectors are already queuing outside the door.
A snowman appears on the high street in the middle of summer. It is holding a sign that reads 'Please stop asking'.
A fisherman catches a boot instead of a fish. He has named the boot and taken it to the pub for a drink.
The city's oldest resident turns 102 and celebrates by beating the council in a game of bowls.
A traffic warden is reported to have been seen smiling. Officials are investigating whether this is a legal offence.
A tiny museum opens in a bus shelter, displaying one very old ticket and a bench from 1961.
A council worker is thanked for twenty years of service. He asks for a new chair and is given a certificate instead.
The bakery's new croissant is so flaky that three customers have been unable to leave the shop without a napkin tattoo.
Crowds gather to watch a man try to balance a bus on his head. He manages six seconds, which is a city record.
A chorus of frogs takes over the reservoir for an evening. Residents say it is the most relaxing noise they have ever complained about.
The town's first skyscraper is missing its top floor, which has apparently been taken for a walk by a crane.
A grocer offers a free apple to anyone who can name all the councillors. Sales are poor, but the apple is always fresh.
Local gardeners compete to grow the largest marrow. The winner says the secret is talking to it and never mentioning the council.
A crane operator waves at a pigeon all afternoon, and the pigeon is said to be the only one who waves back.
Two rival barbers open shops across the street from each other. Both now have longer queues than the post office.
A lost tourist finds a secret tunnel under the market and emerges in the mayor's office. The mayor says he is not surprised.
A fire engine is spotted taking a shortcut through the park. Nobody has been able to say whether it was an emergency or a picnic.
The city's first ice cream van has been found parked on the motorway. Its driver says he is simply following the sunshine.
A parrot escapes from a shop on Market Street and is found reciting the council's full budget report, slightly out of order.
An elderly couple celebrate their sixtieth anniversary by taking the first tram of the day and getting off at the wrong stop.
A library book is returned after fifty years, with a note that says 'It was excellent, sorry about the stains'.
A mysterious pile of carrots appears outside the school gates every Tuesday. Nobody has admitted to leaving them.
The local cricket team loses to a team of seagulls. The seagulls have asked for a rematch in the bins.
A long-lost cat returns home after three years, having apparently been running the bakery across town.
An inventor shows off a machine that cleans the streets by itself. It cleans the streets, then cleans the inventor, then stops.
A town council meeting is interrupted by a passing brass band. The band is invited to stay and asked to be quieter.
A hedgehog is found asleep in the mayor's briefcase. It has been granted a temporary seat on the planning committee.
Local shopkeepers hold a sale on everything that is not nailed down. Nails are reportedly up 40 percent.
A weather balloon lands in the duck pond and the ducks are asked to sign for it.
An ice cream van plays its jingle at 3 a.m. Residents still cannot agree whether it was a dream.
A museum curator wins an award for dusting the same statue for thirty years. The statue has asked to be dusted less.
A cyclist races a tram across the city and loses by one traffic light. He is demanding a rematch and a shower.
Postal workers strike over a missing biscuit. The biscuit is later found in a parcel addressed to the council.
Shopping centre installs a fountain that spouts orange juice. Dentists are cautiously optimistic.
A helium balloon festival ends when every balloon in the city decides to visit the same tree.
Experts reveal that the city's most common sound is a neighbour apologising to a dog.
The council votes unanimously to name the new bridge after a pigeon. The pigeon has not yet been informed.
A tyre factory opens behind the homes on Elm Row. Residents report their washing is turning black on the line.
A new chemical works goes up next to the estate. The bins now have a faint smell of vinegar and regret.
Factory noise keeps the night shift awake and the day shift grumpy. Both shifts have started a petition.
The park now borders the houses on Rose Lane. Residents are planting window boxes and calling the council a hero.
Children from the new flats can reach the park in one minute. Parents report calmer evenings and fewer scraped knees.
Corner shops and houses now share the same street. The bread arrives while it is still warm.
A busy shop opens right under the bedroom windows. Residents say the delivery lorries start before the birds.
A noisy night market is built beside the park. The ducks have moved to the reservoir in protest.
A new school stands next to the family houses. Parents can wave goodbye from the kitchen window.
The school bell now rings through the bedrooms at 7 a.m. Residents want it moved, or at least quieter.
A bus depot is built next to the school gates. Teachers have added a diesel warning to the morning register.
A bus stop opens outside the school. Parents say the children are now arriving on time, a first in living memory.
A hospital opens within walking distance of the old estate. Elderly residents say they feel safer already.
The new hospital car park fills the street with cars all day. Residents are demanding a second car park for the cars.
A café opens beside the hospital entrance. Visitors say the tea has never been so comforting, or so expensive.
A bus stop is placed at the hospital entrance. Patients now get there without a taxi and without a second heart attack.
A fire station opens on the high street. Shopkeepers say the insurance quotes look a lot friendlier already.
A fire station sits next to the factory. Engineers are relieved and the fire crew is trying not to look smug.
A police station is built on the corner of the estate. Residents say the street lamps have started working again.
Police officers now patrol the park by bicycle. The joggers have adopted a constable as a mascot.
The new stadium stands next to the park. Picnickers are reporting an unexpected amount of flying chips.
A bus stop is placed by the stadium. Match-day fans are arriving before kick-off, and the pubs are thrilled.
Crowds from the stadium now clog the road outside the hospital. Ambulance drivers have started honking back.
An airport goes up next to the factory estate. Engineers say the jet fumes and the chimney smoke get along surprisingly well.
A runway is laid beside the park. The kite club has moved two kilometres away and is very sorry about it.
The airport is now beside the hospital. Surgeons have asked for quieter flight paths during operations.
The landfill and the factory now share a fence. The seagulls have asked for a joint pension scheme.
A landfill is placed beside the park. The picnic benches now have a view of the rubbish mountain.
A power plant rises beside the factories. Factory bosses say the electricity bill is down and the cloud is up.
A power plant towers over the park. Children now draw it as a giant friendly robot and the council is calling it public art.
A water tower stands beside the park. Joggers can now refill their bottles in the middle of their laps.
A water tower is built next to the industrial estate. Factory managers report the taps are running clean and brown-free.
A water tower sits beside the school. Pupils have started a tally of how many drinks of water they can have a day.
A rail depot is built beside the factories. Freight trains now load right at the factory gate, and the lorry drivers are looking for work.
A rail depot is placed next to the school. Teachers have started speaking louder than the shunting engines, which is exhausting.
A rail depot sits beside the hospital. Doctors have asked for the trains to hoot softly during night shifts.
The bus depot is placed beside the park. Joggers are reporting exhaust fumes at the top of every lap.
A bus depot is built next to the factories. Workers now have a ride to the gates and nobody is walking in the rain.
A bus depot is placed beside the school. The buses now leave the yard in a neat line and the children clap.
A tram depot is built beside the houses. The trams are quiet, clean, and the first one rings a cheerful good morning.
The tram depot is placed beside the factory. Trams now carry soot as well as passengers, and nobody has the heart to tell the tram.
A tram depot is built by the shops. Customers are arriving by tram, and the shopkeepers are dusting off the welcome mats.
A taxi depot opens beside the shopping street. The drivers are eating at the café and calling it a good day.
A taxi depot is built beside the houses. Late-night taxi horns have become the neighbourhood's new alarm clock.
A taxi depot sits beside the hospital. Night nurses can now get home without waiting in the cold.
A taxi depot opens by the airport. Tourists are finally getting a ride without a three-hour argument over the price.
A bus stop is placed at the end of the terrace. The commute is shorter, the shelter is dry, and the bench has been named.
A bus stop opens beside the park. The buses are full of picnickers on Sunday and empty of excuses on Monday.
A bus stop opens at the factory gate. Workers say the walk to work has gone from forty minutes to four.
A bus stop is placed outside the shopping centre. Shoppers are arriving by the busload and the car park is finally quiet.
A bus stop is placed beside the school. Pupils have discovered that the bench is perfect for a long chat during registration.
A police station opens next to the school. The lollipop lady now has a constable to help her cross the road.
A police station is built beside the factories. The workers have started a rota of gentle protests outside the front desk.
A fire station opens by the park. Children are thrilled to see the engines wash, and the fire crew have started a barbecue club.
A fire station is built beside the school. Pupils now know exactly where the engines live, and they keep asking to visit.
A fire station sits next to the hospital. The ambulance and fire crews have started a shared tea rota.
A new park opens beside the shops. Ice cream sales are through the roof and the car park is finally empty.
The park is built right beside the school. Lessons now start ten minutes late every day because the playground is simply too good to leave.
A small park opens across from the hospital. Patients are sitting out in the sun, and the nurses say they are less grumpy.
A bus stop opens beside the park. Commuters now wait for the bus among the flowers, and the bus is nearly always on time.
Shops are built right next to the factory gates. Workers now have a sandwich on the walk home, and the bakers are very happy.
A late-night takeaway opens beside the school. Teachers are asking if the chip shop can close at four, please.
A chemist and a café open beside the hospital. The waiting room is quieter and the prescriptions are finally in stock.
A new shopping parade is placed beside the stadium. Match-day tickets are now sold alongside sausage rolls and parking fines.
Two factories are placed side by side. The supply lorries now share a loading bay and nobody is arguing about the parking.
A new factory opens beside a bus stop. The shift workers are finally arriving on time, and so is the bus.
A factory is built within sight of the school. Children have started drawing the chimney, and the drawings are unflattering.
Jobs arrive as a factory opens next to the new houses. Residents are walking to work and the bakery is busy again.
A factory opens next to the park and creates forty new jobs. The park is quieter, but the payslips are louder.
A factory opens beside the hospital. Surgeons have started wearing masks in the car park, which is not a good sign.
New houses are built in a tidy row beside the old ones. The street has a new name, Neighbour Road, and nobody argued.
A hospital is placed right beside the new homes. Parents can reach the maternity ward on foot, and the first babies have arrived.
The stadium is built beside the new estate. Fans are walking home past the bakeries, and the bakers are on their third oven.
A police station is built beside the estate. The houses on the corner have stopped locking their bikes.
The new fire station stands on the edge of the estate. The residents have asked for a bell to hear the engines leave.
The landfill sits on the edge of the estate. The houses now come with a free view of the rubbish mountain.
A power plant is built beside the houses. The lights are on all night, and so is the hum.
The airport is extended towards the estate. Residents have rebranded their gardens as acoustic test areas.
Stadium floodlights are switched on at midnight. The residents are seeing the match from their bedrooms, for free.
A rail depot opens next to the estate. Commuters are catching the early train without a single bus, and the trains are on time.
A tram depot opens near the houses. Residents have a tram every five minutes and the neighbours have started waving.
A taxi depot is built beside the estate. The night-shift workers can now get home in minutes, and the drivers have a café.
A bus stop is placed beside the estate. The retired couple at number 12 has already caught the 9.15 every day this week.
A school is built beside the houses. Parents are cancelling their cars and the children are arriving with muddy knees and happy faces.
The bus depot is placed next to the houses. Residents have started pre-warming their coffee to match the morning engines.
A new shopping centre is built beside the houses. The car park lights shine straight into the bedrooms until dawn.
A rooftop garden on the old post office is opened and the bees are already demanding a bigger share of the honey.
A bored councillor counts every lamp post in the city and finds exactly one that is still a little bit crooked.
A visitor from the countryside asks where the cows are. The city council says they are in the budget, somewhere.
A sudden burst of confetti falls over the high street. Officials say it was an accident, the confetti is not so sure.
Mysterious chalk drawings of rockets appear on every pavement overnight. The art teacher says they are very good, and very illegal.
A market stallholder sells a mirror to a man who says it is the only one that still shows him as a younger man.
Residents hold a midnight picnic on the motorway. The police arrive, look at the cake, and take a slice.
A bread van is seen speeding through the city, leaving a trail of warm rolls. Bakers say it is a marketing stunt, the rolls say nothing.
A school choir records a song about recycling. It is so catchy that the bins have started humming along.
Local pensioners challenge teenagers to a game of skipping. The score is currently eleven hips to one.
A cloud of bees swarms the post office. The postmaster says the letters are still going out, just more slowly.
A car wash opens near the reservoir and offers a free rubber duck with every visit. Sales of rubber ducks have tripled.
Two rival hot dog sellers reach a peace deal over the high street and sell a combined mustard-ketchup stall.
A museum announces it has found a dinosaur bone under the car park. The car park has been turned into a dig, and the parking fines are paying for it.
A weather station reports that the rain has been measured twice today, once by the sensor and once by a pensioner's umbrella.
A new park gives the old town square some much-needed shade. The benches are full before the ribbon is even cut.
The city's newest park has a playground, a pond, and a ten-metre slide. The council is not allowed to say how much it cost.
Dog walkers are delighted with the new park. The dogs are less delighted, because they now have to share it with joggers.
A small park opens between the flats and the shops. Residents say it is the first place in years where they have stopped to talk.
Pensioners claim the best bench in the new park, and will not be moved for any reason.
The new school has a garden, a library corner, and a stage. The head teacher says the drama club has already claimed the stage.
Children from the far estate no longer have to walk two miles. The new school opens with a bouncy castle and a headache for the caterers.
The school gates open to a crowd of excited parents. One dad is already writing a letter to the council asking for a second school.
A brand-new school welcomes its first pupils. The school crest was designed by a six-year-old and is mostly a dinosaur.
The new hospital has its first birth on the first morning. The baby is named after the planning committee chair.
The hospital's new wing opens with more beds and a much quieter waiting room. Nurses are still learning where the new kettle is.
Patients are arriving from across the region, and the hospital car park is already full. The council is buying more spaces.
The new library has a reading room with a view of the river. A regular says she has finally found a reason to stop reading on her phone.
Children's story time is packed out at the new library. The puppets are sharing the stage with a very sleepy pigeon.
The stadium is open for its first match. The scoreboard works, the seats are comfortable, and the crowd has already lost its voice.
Season ticket sales break every record at the new stadium. The club secretary is trying to remember where he put his pen.
The city's surplus is big enough to repair every pothole on Market Street. The potholes have been informed.
Treasury reports a spare million for next year. The council is already promising to spend it on three different things.
The number of stolen bikes falls to its lowest level in ten years. Cyclists are reportedly leaving their bikes unlocked out of sheer confidence.
The neighbourhood watch reports an empty week for the first time since records began. They are now bored and slightly disappointed.
One thousand residents, one brass band, and a very confused cat who has been declared the official welcoming committee.
The city hits ten thousand people. The council has finally needed a second traffic light, and the first one is thrilled.
Fifty thousand residents now call the city home. The bakers are baking bigger loaves and the buses are running fuller.
New job numbers are out and every shop on the high street is hiring. The shop windows are full of handwritten vacancy notes.
A record number of residents are in work. The job centre has put up a sign saying, 'Nothing to see here, come back never'.
The local pub reports a surge in happy hour customers. The landlord says he has never been so pleased to pour a drink.
Residents report their neighbours are waving more often. Psychologists are calling it the Good Morning Effect.
The new bus network goes live across the city. The first passenger on the first route thanks the driver by name, which he never gets.
A new tram line rolls out of the depot to cheers and a brass band. The tram has been painted green, which the children approve of.
The new bus depot is ready to take on the morning rush. Its first fleet of buses are polished, fuelled, and slightly nervous.
The rail depot opens its turntable to the public for the first time. Children queue for a picture and the engine driver waves.
The tram depot opens to visitors who want to see the trams wash. The cleaning crew has agreed to make it a weekly show.
The taxi depot is open for business with a new radio system. Drivers say the calls are coming through quicker and the jokes are coming through slower.
A new bus stop opens on the far side of the estate. Pensioners are celebrating with the first ride to the seaside.
A bus stop is placed outside the old people's home. The residents have started a timetable of their own, which is more accurate.
Power demand dips and the grid has spare energy to spare. Engineers have turned on every light in the town hall, just to be sure.
The water tower is full to the brim, and the reservoir is overflowing. Local gardeners are rejoicing and the hosepipe ban is the first to go.
Every plot in the new estate has a family in it. The removal lorries are finally getting a rest.
The shops on the new parade have all opened. The first shopper asks for a receipt, and the shopkeeper cries.
Every factory unit is now in use. The forklift drivers have started a friendly race between the loading bays.
Morning traffic clears the bridge in record time. The bridge is so surprised that it has stopped creaking.
New flats are listed at prices a nurse can afford. The estate agent has been asked to come down and explain it.
A poll shows the mayor's popularity is up, mainly among people who have only seen the new park.
The last of the flood defences are finished. The riverside cafés have reopened and the ducks have returned to the pond.
The city-wide clean-up ends with a litter-picking parade. The mayor carries the biggest bag and a single, stubborn sock.
Two hundred saplings go into the ground along the canal. The gardeners ask people to come back in twenty years and say thank you.
The river is clear enough to see the bottom. A kingfisher has moved in and is refusing to leave.
Every pupil in the final year passes their exams this summer. The head teacher has promised a half-day holiday for the staff, who are not yet awake.
The air monitors on Mill Road read higher than ever. The local bakery has moved its ovens to the roof to keep the smell out.
The smog is so thick that the buses have turned on their fog lights at noon. The drivers say it looks like the end of the world.
Roadworks and a broken-down lorry create a jam all the way back to the reservoir. The lorry driver has offered tea to everyone stuck behind him.
The motorway slip road is blocked for the third time this week. Drivers now know the traffic report by heart and are still stuck.
The council is cancelling the summer fair to save money. The fair committee has responded by holding a funeral for the bunting.
A budget cut means the library will open two days less. The librarians have started reading aloud to passers-by in protest.
Shops on the high street report a run of break-ins overnight. The shopkeepers have put up signs asking the thieves to at least leave the biscuits.
A car is stolen from outside the post office and found the next day parked outside the town hall. Councillors say they are taking it personally.
A chip pan fire on the corner of Church Street sends smoke over three roads. Nobody was hurt, but the chip shop owner is in shock.
A factory fire draws a crowd of onlookers. Several people take photos, and the firefighters ask them to please go home.
The power goes out during the evening football match. Fans listen to the game on a battery radio and the pub starts a sing-along.
A substation fault leaves the east side in the dark for six hours. The bakers are working by candlelight and the bread is slightly gothic.
The reservoir level drops for the third week in a row. Councillors have asked residents to use the bath for two, not for one.
Factory closures leave dozens out of work this month. The job centre has run out of forms and is photocopying them by hand.
Jobless figures rise again. The local café has started a free breakfast for anyone who has been looking all week.
Bin collectors walk out over pay. Rubbish is piling up on every street and the seagulls are holding a meeting of their own.
The tram drivers begin an overtime ban. The trams still run, but only at the speed of the slowest tram driver.
The landfill has reached capacity and the council is asking the public to recycle their old sofas. Nobody is sure where the old sofas will go.
The river breaks its banks on the lower road. Sandbags are being stacked outside every front door and the ducks are very pleased.
Heavy rain floods the underpass and a bus gets stuck. The passengers are rescued by a rowing club, which is very proud of itself.
Residents rank the city's potholes as their number one concern. The potholes are yet to respond to the survey.
A survey finds the most common complaint is that nothing ever happens. The council says it is a sign of stability.
Rent on the Riverside flats goes up again. The tenants have organised a picnic outside the landlord's office.
The factory chimney releases a plume that drifts over the school playground. The headteacher cancels break for the second time this week.
Night shifts at the factory keep the whole street awake. One resident has started knocking on the factory gate with a rolling pin.
A sewage pipe bursts beside the market. The stallholders have moved their fish to the other side of town.
The road outside the school sinks by a metre overnight. The school bus now has to take a detour through the cricket pitch.
A new bus route is so quiet that the driver has started playing chess with the only passenger. The score is level.
More people are sleeping rough near the station. Volunteers are handing out blankets and hot drinks every night.
A council audit finds a stack of unpaid parking fines in the mayor's office. The mayor says they were for his car, which he is sure was legally parked.
The bus company is in trouble and is asking passengers to pay with spare change. The change is being counted in the car park.
A pile of old tyres is found by the canal. The council has asked the public to report any more, and the public has sent photos of their own tyres.
A tram comes off its rails at the junction and blocks the bridge for a day. Commuters are now walking the bridge, which the bridge does not enjoy.
A fire starts in the bus depot workshop. The mechanics pull three buses out of the flames and the coffee urn is lost.
Three buses break down on the same route in one afternoon. The depot has asked the buses to stop talking to each other.
A new factory brings jobs to the estate next door. Residents are happy with the paychecks and are learning to live with the smell.
A park has been built so close to the houses that the football goes through the bedroom windows every Saturday.
The new shopping parade has turned the park into a car park. The swings are still there, but nobody can reach them.
The factory next to the school offers a job-shadowing day. Pupils come home covered in grease and very keen on engineering.
The school and park share a fence now. Pupils have started picnics on the grass and the staff have started copying them.
A factory next to the hospital starts making face masks. The nurses are very grateful, and very sick of the colour blue.
The park beside the hospital is so popular that the ambulances are struggling to reach the entrance on weekends.
The bus depot gives the estate the best bus service in town. The residents have sent the drivers a box of biscuits.
The bus depot's morning queue blocks the shop doors. The baker says he cannot get his delivery van past the buses.
A new rail depot brings a fast line into the city and the estate's house prices climb. Residents are pretending they are not pleased.
A rail depot opens beside the park and the new station is bringing visitors in every weekend. The ice cream van has relocated to the platform.
The rail depot's delivery lorries are blocking the shop loading bays. The shopkeepers have started charging the trains a parking fee.
Cheaper electricity arrives for the homes beside the new power plant. The residents are paying less and complaining more, which is traditional.
The water tower is repainted with a giant advert for toothpaste. Residents are not sure how they feel about being sold to from above.
The stadium crowds have made the cafés beside it sell out of tea. The baristas have been asked to start selling beer, and they are not happy about it.
The airport brings a new hotel to the estate, and the residents' spare rooms are suddenly worth a fortune.
The airport's car park has pushed the shops out of their parking spaces. The shopkeepers are calling it the great parking war.
The landfill beside the estate has been capped and landscaped. The residents have a new hill to walk up, and the view is not bad.
The fire station's siren is tested at noon in the park. The picnickers have agreed to bring earplugs next time.
A police station is built on the estate, and the late-night patrol cars are a little too loud for the nearby children.
The police station sits beside the shop row, and the shoplifters have simply moved to the next street.
The tram depot is so close to the park that the depot's bells are the first thing picnickers hear on a Sunday morning.
A tram depot opens beside the school. Pupils now arrive by tram, and the drivers ring a cheerful bell at the gates.
The taxi depot has turned the park entrance into a queue of idling cars. The joggers say the exhaust has made the run feel longer.
The bus stop beside the hospital is always full. Patients say they cannot sit down, and the bench is only for the staff.
A bus stop is placed under the bedroom window of number 9. The bus driver has become a known nuisance on the street.
The shopping parade beside the school has a stationery shop. Parents are getting school supplies in the same trip as their milk.
The park is so popular that the houses on the corner have been turned into a cafe for dog owners. The dogs are not paying rent.
The corner shop opens right beside the terrace. Residents can walk for milk in their slippers, and most of them do.
A factory beside the school sponsors the new science lab. The pupils have named the lab after the factory's oldest machine.
The hospital and school share a car park, which fills every morning at drop-off. Doctors and parents are now at war over the last space.
The stadium is next to the school and the match-day noise starts during maths. The maths teacher has started using the goal chants in his lessons.
The stadium and park are neighbours now, and the fans are picnicking on the grass before kick-off. The park has never been busier.
The airport's new viewing platform is built beside the park. Families are picnicking and cheering every landing with their sandwiches in the air.
The power plant sponsors a new school computer room. The pupils have stopped drawing the chimney and started drawing the computers.
The landfill's new access road runs past the school gate. The children are learning about recycling by watching lorries go past.
The fire station's new training yard sits beside the factory, and the crews are practising rescues on the factory's loading dock.
A water tower stands over the shopping street, and the cafés now serve the cleanest tea in the city.
A water tower is built beside the hospital. Surgeons say the sterilising water has never been so clean.
The water tower is repainted with a giant face by the local art club. The school says the face is staring straight at the maths block.
Factory lorries are queueing down the high street. The shopkeepers have started charging the drivers for the parking spaces.
The factory's lunchtime fumes drift across the park. The picnickers have moved to the far side and are sulking.
A new factory brings a medical supply contract to the hospital next door. The porters are delighted to have the shortest delivery route in town.
The bus depot's morning queue blocks the factory gate. The workers have started to walk and the buses are quietly mocked.
The bus depot's diesel fumes drift towards the school field. The gardeners have stopped planting near the fence.
The rail depot's shunting yard blocks the road to the factory. The lorry drivers have started a very quiet protest with their horns.
A tram depot is built right beside the estate, and the tram bells start at six. The residents have asked for a snooze button.
A tram depot opens beside the hospital. Visitors arrive by tram, and the car park is finally quiet enough to hear the birds.
A taxi depot opens by the factory gates, and the night-shift workers are getting home in minutes instead of hours.
The taxi depot sits next to the school gates. Teachers are patrolling the pavement with whistles and very short tempers.
A bus stop is placed at the factory gate, and the queue spills onto the main road. The bus driver has asked the factory to move its gate.
The park bus stop is so busy that the picnic blankets now have to share the pavement with the commuters.
The shopping centre bus stop has become a meeting point for the entire town. Nobody has bought anything for an hour.
A bus stop beside the school means the pupils leave on time. The bus driver has learned all their names, and most of their dogs.
The police station opens next to the school and the school's pupils have started a slow-motion protest against the sirens.
The police station's car park has taken over the park's football pitch. The goalkeepers now stand next to the bollards.
The fire station's new bell rings at seven each morning, to the delight of the children and the fury of their parents.
The fire station's engines block the shopping street every time there is a drill. Shopkeepers are demanding a second fire station on the other side.
A new park opens with a skate ramp, and the teenagers who asked for it are now the most responsible people in town.
The new school's first assembly includes a choir, a magician, and a talk on the importance of bins. The bins were not impressed by the talk.
The hospital's new cafe serves the best soup in the district. Doctors say it is the only medicine that works on a Monday.
Floodlights are switched on at the new stadium. The residents of the nearby flats say they can finally read in bed without a lamp.
A rare surplus has council officers counting their pens with a smile. They are being asked not to celebrate in the corridors.
The local gardening club reports a record turnout, and every single volunteer has said they will be back next week.
A new transit route is finished, and the first passenger to get a seat on the top deck says it is the best view in the city.
Morning traffic flows so well that drivers are arriving at work early and having to wait outside the office.
Air quality falls again over the industrial east side. The runners' club has moved its Saturday run to the hills.
Police report the quietest weekend of the year, which they describe as a worry in itself because they have nothing to do.
The job fair on Market Square is so busy that the stallholders have run out of pens and the employers are using their own.
A new park opens across the road from the estate, and the residents' children have made it their second home.
A bus stop opens outside the shopping parade. Shoppers say they can carry four bags on the bus, which is a revolution.
A school is placed beside the hospital, and the nurses are teaching first aid in the playground. The pupils are very good at bandages.
A new factory opens next to the estate. Residents are sorting their laundry by colour and smell, and the laundry is not impressed.
The bus stop beside the park has attracted so many buses that the geese have declared a no-fly zone.
The stadium has been built next to the estate, and the residents are selling cold drinks from their front gardens on match days.
The hospital's new helipad is built above the estate. The residents have started wearing hats to the shops.
Dust from the factory yard settles on the school's new playground. The pupils are calling it snow, and the caretaker is calling it a bill.
The factory has agreed to plant trees along the park border. The first saplings are already taller than the foreman.
The park's new fountain is switched on for the first time, and a sudden gust sends the mayor's hat straight into it.
The school's first lunch menu is published, and parents are amazed that the pudding is listed as a food group.
The city has officially grown up. The mayor celebrates by unlocking new buildings and immediately pretending this was the plan all along.
Population milestone reached. Planners say it was careful growth; residents say it was mostly the roads going everywhere at once.
A new milestone for the city, and a cheque from the regional government. City Hall has already spent it twice, in theory.
The treasury is officially empty. The mayor has been seen checking down the back of the council chamber sofa.
City Hall is broke. Advisers recommend raising taxes, cutting spending or, failing that, a very large bake sale.
The city takes out a loan. The bank manager smiles politely and adds the mayor to the special list.
